name: Triceps brachii
func: The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm. It straightens the elbow, powering pushing movements like push-ups, throwing and getting up from a chair.

levels.kid:
Your **triceps** is the muscle on the **back** of your upper arm. "Tri" means three, because it has **three parts** at the top that join together.

The biceps on the front bends your elbow. The triceps does the opposite: it **straightens your elbow**. So when you push a door, do a push-up, throw a ball or push yourself up out of a chair, your triceps is doing the work.

It is actually bigger than the biceps! It makes up about two-thirds of the muscle in your upper arm.
levels.hs:
The **triceps brachii** occupies the whole **back (posterior compartment)** of the upper arm and is the main **extensor of the elbow**. It is larger than the biceps.

It has three heads:
The **long head** starts on the **infraglenoid tubercle** of the scapula, just below the shoulder socket, so it also crosses the shoulder.
The **lateral head** starts on the back of the humerus above the **radial groove**.
The **medial head** starts on the back of the humerus below the radial groove and lies deepest.

All three join into a strong tendon that inserts on the **olecranon** of the ulna, the bony point of the elbow.

Its main action is **extending the elbow**. The long head also helps **extend and adduct** the arm at the shoulder.

It is supplied by the **radial nerve** (mainly C6–C8, especially C7), which spirals around the back of the humerus in the **radial groove**, between the lateral and medial heads, together with the **profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery**. Tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon produces the **triceps reflex**, which tests mainly **C7**.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** long head from the infraglenoid tubercle; lateral head from the posterior humerus superior and lateral to the radial groove; medial head from the posterior humerus inferior and medial to the radial groove and the intermuscular septa. Insertion: the proximal posterior **olecranon** and the deep fascia of the forearm. The small **anconeus** muscle, lateral to the olecranon, assists extension and is functionally continuous with the medial head.

**Spaces of the posterior shoulder:** the long head of triceps separates the **quadrangular space** (axillary nerve, posterior circumflex humeral artery) from the **triangular space** (circumflex scapular artery) above, and with the humerus bounds the **triangular interval** (radial nerve and profunda brachii artery) below teres major.

**Recruitment:** the **medial head** is the workhorse, active in almost all extension; the lateral and long heads join when more force is needed. The long head's force also depends on shoulder position, being strongest with the shoulder flexed (overhead).

**Innervation:** the **radial nerve** gives branches to each head; branches to the long and medial heads arise in the axilla, before the nerve enters the radial groove, which partly protects triceps function in mid-shaft fractures. The **ulnar collateral nerve**, a radial branch to the medial head, travels beside the ulnar nerve.

**Blood supply:** the **profunda brachii artery** and superior ulnar collateral artery, plus posterior circumflex humeral branches to the long head.

**Relations:** the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, just medial to the triceps insertion, and the radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to reach the front of the arm.
levels.phd:
The triceps is a classic **bi-articular versus mono-articular** model. The long head crosses both shoulder and elbow, allowing energy to be transferred between joints, for example during throwing, where shoulder flexion stretches the long head while the elbow extends. The mono-articular medial and lateral heads produce elbow torque independent of shoulder position.

Architecturally, the heads differ. The lateral head has relatively long fascicles and high power potential; the medial head contains a higher proportion of **type I** (slow) fibres, consistent with its tonic, low-force role, while the long and lateral heads have more **type II** fibres. Values vary between individuals and studies.

The **triceps reflex** is a monosynaptic stretch reflex: tendon tap stretches muscle spindles, **Ia afferents** fire, and they excite alpha motor neurons in the C7 (and C6, C8) ventral horn directly. Reciprocal inhibition of the biceps occurs through Ia inhibitory interneurons.

Clinically important research involves **nerve transfers**. In C5–C6 brachial plexus injuries, a triceps branch of the radial nerve (usually to the long head or medial head) can be transferred to the anterior division of the **axillary nerve** to restore deltoid function, the Somsak/Leechavengvongs transfer. This works because the triceps has redundant branches and losing one causes little loss of extension.

In tetraplegia, where the triceps may be paralysed while the deltoid works, the **posterior deltoid-to-triceps transfer** restores elbow extension, important for transferring from a wheelchair and reaching overhead.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** test elbow extension against resistance from a flexed position, and the **triceps reflex (C7)**. Absent triceps reflex with weak extension, wrist flexion and finger extension, plus numbness of the middle finger, suggests **C7 radiculopathy**, the most common cervical radiculopathy.

**Radial nerve injury localisation:**
In the **axilla** (for example from badly fitted crutches): weak triceps plus wrist drop.
In **mid-shaft humerus fractures** (radial groove): the nerve is injured in about 10%; the triceps is usually **spared** or only partly weak because its branches arise higher. The result is **wrist drop** with numbness over the dorsal first web space. Most cases recover with observation.
**Posterior interosseous nerve** lesions at the elbow: finger drop without sensory loss or triceps weakness.

**Triceps tendon rupture** is rare: a fall on an outstretched hand with sudden forced flexion. Look for a palpable gap above the olecranon, inability to extend against gravity, and a small avulsed bony fleck on a lateral X-ray (the "flake sign"). Complete tears are usually repaired surgically.

**Olecranon fractures** disrupt the extensor mechanism and often need tension-band wiring or plating. **Olecranon bursitis** causes a soft swelling over the point of the elbow, sometimes infected.

In **upper motor neuron lesions** such as stroke, the arm often adopts a flexed posture because flexors overpower the weakened triceps. In spinal cord injury, preserved triceps function (C7) is a major milestone for independent transfers.

keyPoints: Inserts on the olecranon of the ulna
Main extensor of the elbow; long head also extends the shoulder
Radial nerve; triceps reflex tests C7
Mid-shaft humerus fractures can cause wrist drop but usually spare triceps

test.q: Where does the triceps brachii insert?
test.explain: The triceps tendon attaches to the olecranon, the point of the elbow.
The radial nerve runs in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads.

test.q: The triceps reflex mainly tests which root?
test.explain: The triceps reflex is mostly C7.

test.q: Which head of triceps also crosses the shoulder joint?
test.explain: The long head arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.

test.q: A mid-shaft humerus fracture with a radial nerve injury typically causes wrist ______.
test.explain: The wrist extensors are paralysed, but triceps is usually spared.
